ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Old English foran Old English beforan Middle English bifore English before Inherited from Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian befoar (“before”), German Low German bevör (“before”), German bevor (“before”).

ex: I want this done before Monday.
We made an odd party before the arrival of the Ten, particularly when the Celebrity dropped in for lunch or dinner.
He stood before me.
We sat before the fire to warm ourselves.
He performed before the troops in North Africa.
He spoke before a joint session of Congress.
The case laid before the panel aroused nothing but ridicule.
If a suit be begun before an archdeacon[…]

senses.d: In store for, in the future of (someone).
ex: Your whole life is before you.
The golden age[…]is before us.

senses.d: In front of, according to a formal system of ordering items.
ex: In alphabetical order, "cat" comes before "dog", "canine" before feline".

senses.d: At a higher or greater position than, in a ranking.
ex: An entrepreneur puts market share and profit before quality, and amateur intrinsic qualities before economical considerations.
He that cometh after me is preferred before me.
I've never done this before.
This achievement far exceeded anything that had come before.

senses.d: In advance in position or sequence; ahead.
ex: We walked behind while they went before.

When people call this beast to mind,
They marvel more and more
At such a little tail behind,
So LARGE a trunk before.

senses.d: In advance of the time when.
ex: Near-synonym: no later than
Brush your teeth before you go to bed.
I'll die before I('ll) tell you anything about it.

senses.d: Of before-and-after images: the one that shows the difference before a specified treatment.
That which occurred or existed previously.
ex: We talk about all the befores. The stupid things we did. The funny things. The times she made us laugh.

grp.label: in advance of the time when

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French avant, from Old French avant (“before, prior in time, forward”), from Late Latin ab ante (“before, in front of”), from Latin ab (“from”) + ante (“before”).

Literally, “of front”.

ety.text: From Middle English biforhand, biforhond, beforehonde, bifornhand, equivalent to before + hand. [13th century. After Old French avant main].

senses.d: At an earlier or preceding time.
ex: Will it be possible to have access to the room beforehand so that we can set up chairs?
I love playing tennis but I always get so nervous beforehand.

senses.d: In comfortable circumstances as regards property; forehanded.
ex: rich and much beforehand

senses.d: In a state of anticipation or preoccupation.
ex: Agricola […] resolves to be beforehand with the danger.
The last cited author has been beforehand with me.
